In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[number theory]], a '''Cunningham number''' is a certain kind of [[integer]] named after English mathematician [[Allan Joseph Champneys Cunningham|A. J. C. Cunningham]].

==Definition==

Cunningham numbers are a simple type of [[binomial number]] – they are of the form

:<math>b^n\pm1</math>

where ''b'' and ''n'' are integers and ''b'' is not a [[perfect power]].  They are denoted ''C''<sup>±</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n'').

==Terms==

The Cunningham numbers are:

:3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 15, 17, 24, 26, 28, 31, 33, 35, 37, 48, 50, 63, 65, 80, 82, 99, 101, 120, 122, 124, 126, 127, 129, 143, 145, 168, 170, 195, 197, ... {{OEIS|A080262}}

The Cunningham numbers ''C''<sup>−</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n'') are:

:3, 7, 8, 15, 24, 26, 31, 35, 48, 63, 80, 99, 120, 124, 127, 143, 168, 195, 215, 224, 242, 255, 288, 323, 342, 360, 399, 440, 483, ... {{OEIS|A045542}}

The Cunningham numbers ''C''<sup>+</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n'') are:

:5, 9, 10, 17, 26, 28, 33, 37, 50, 65, 82, 101, 122, 126, 129, 145, 170, 197, 217, 226, 244, 257, 290, 325, 344, 362, 401, 442, 485, ... {{OEIS|A216765}}

It is conjectured that 26 is the only number that is both a Cunningham number ''C''<sup>−</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n'') and a Cunningham number ''C''<sup>+</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n''), this conjecture is equivalent to that 25 and 27 are the only two [[perfect power]]s differ by 2 (see [[Pillai's conjecture]]). Note that the proven [[Catalan's conjecture]] is that 8 and 9 are the only two [[perfect power]]s differ by 1.

==Properties==
* There are infinitely many [[Parity (mathematics)|even and odd]] Cunningham numbers. Provable through observation that the infinite series <math>6^n\pm1</math> and <math>5^n\pm1</math> are both contained within the Cunningham numbers, and contain only odd and even numbers respectively.
** By the same logic, there are infinitely many Cunningham numbers which are 5 [[Modulo (mathematics)|modulo]] 10, 7 modulo 10, 4 modulo 10, or 6 modulo 10. In fact, for every [[Integers mod n|modulo number]] <math>n<36</math>, there are infinitely many Cunningham numbers congruent to every residue mod <math>n</math>, however, for <math>n=36</math>, there is no Cunningham number congruent to 11, 13, 23, or 25 mod 36, this is because for the numbers ''m'' = 11, 13, 23, or 25 mod 36, neither ''m''+1 nor ''m''−1 can be [[powerful number|powerful]].
* Although by the proven [[Catalan's conjecture]], 8 and 9 are the only two Cunningham numbers that are [[perfect power]]s, there are infinitely many Cunningham numbers that are [[powerful number]]s, since if ''m'' is a Cunningham number ''C''<sup>−</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n'') that is a powerful number (such as 8), then so is <math>4m(m+1)</math>. The first ten such Cunningham numbers are:
** 8 = ''C''<sup>−</sup>(3,2)
** 9 = ''C''<sup>+</sup>(2,3)
** 288 = ''C''<sup>−</sup>(17,2)
** 675 = ''C''<sup>−</sup>(26,2)
** 9800 = ''C''<sup>−</sup>(99,2)
** 12168 = ''C''<sup>+</sup>(23,3)
** 235224 = ''C''<sup>−</sup>(485,2)
** 332928 = ''C''<sup>−</sup>(577,2)
** 465125 = ''C''<sup>+</sup>(682,2)
** 1825200 = ''C''<sup>−</sup>(1351,2)

==Primality==

Establishing whether or not a given Cunningham number is [[prime number|prime]] has been the main focus of research around this type of number.<ref>J. Brillhart, D. H. Lehmer, J. Selfridge, B. Tuckerman, and S. S. Wagstaff Jr., ''Factorizations of b<sup>n</sup>±1, b=2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12 Up to High Powers (n)'', 3rd ed. Providence, RI: Amer. Math. Soc., 1988.</ref>  Two particularly famous families of Cunningham numbers in this respect are the [[Fermat number]]s, which are those of the form ''C''<sup>+</sup>(2,&thinsp;2<sup>''m''</sup>), and the [[Mersenne numbers]], which are those of the form ''C''<sup>−</sup>(2,&thinsp;''p'') with prime ''p''.

The prime Cunningham numbers are:

:3, 5, 7, 17, 31, 37, 101, 127, 197, 257, 401, 577, 677, 1297, 1601, 2917, 3137, 4357, 5477, 7057, 8101, 8191, 8837, ... {{OEIS|A296422}}

In fact, these numbers are exactly the [[generalized Fermat prime]]s (which are those of the form ''C''<sup>+</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;2<sup>''m''</sup>) with even ''b'') and the [[Mersenne prime]]s (which are those of the form ''C''<sup>−</sup>(2,&thinsp;''p'') with prime ''p''), since if the Cunningham number ''C''<sup>−</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n'') is prime, then ''b'' = 2 and ''n'' is prime, and if the Cunningham number ''C''<sup>+</sup>(''b'',&thinsp;''n'') is prime, then ''b'' is even and ''n'' is [[power of 2]], this is because the [[Factorization|algebraic factorization]] of the [[binomial number]]s, such as [[difference of two squares]] and [[sum of two cubes]].

Cunningham worked on gathering together all known data on which of these numbers were prime. In 1925 he published tables which summarised his findings with [[H. J. Woodall]], and much computation has been done in the intervening time to fill these tables.<ref>R. P. Brent and H. J. J. te Riele, ''Factorizations of a<sup>n</sup>±1, 13≤a&lt;100'' Report NM-R9212, Centrum voor Wiskunde en Informatica. Amsterdam, 1992.</ref>
